title: 104 Loyalty Leaders Reveal 5 Lessons Every Brand Needs to Hear
summary: Discover the highlights from The BIG Handshake™ Loyalty Chicago 2026, where 104 loyalty leaders shared honest insights and knowledge.
body_markdown:
On November 10, 104 loyalty leaders filled a room at the Omni Chicago for the first U.S. edition of The BIG Handshake™ Loyalty. We hoped for 60 attendees. We got a full house, 16 speakers, and a day of honest talk about what works in loyalty and what doesn’t. By the end of it, 92% of attendees who answered our survey said they want to come back.


The tone was set early: candid, warm and full of energy. Our MC,


[Lindsay Eichten](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lindsay-eichten-clmp-09a3134/) of Omni Hotels and Resorts, said it plainly: “A loyalty program does not equal loyal customers.” Points and tiers are tools. Real loyalty comes from service, consistency, and keeping your promises.


Every session that followed came back to that idea. Here is what we took home.


## 1. Simple beats clever


Panera had a 15-year-old surprise-and-delight program with more than 70 million members. Over half of them never came often enough to earn a reward. In a fireside chat with


[Mary McGroarty](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mary-mcgroarty-0994a345/) of


[Braze](https://www.braze.com/) (our lead sponsor), Panera’s


[Catherine Thacker](https://www.linkedin.com/in/cthacker/) put it, the program “was definitely feeling more like a surprise and a lot less like a delight.” So Panera rebuilt it around clear value and member choice, and raised the reward rate about four times. Its new MyPanera Mondays lifted Monday traffic so much that the team had to change its sales forecasts.


Great Wolf Lodge did the same with a plain cashback-style program. Spend $10, earn a point worth $1. It now has nearly 5 million members and an **18%** lift in repeat visits, according to


[Dave Van Saun](https://www.linkedin.com/in/vansaun/) . At Audience Rewards, President


[Katie Dalton](https://www.linkedin.com/in/daltonkatiea/) ‘s team stopped saying “earn 1,000 points” and started saying “earn free Broadway tickets.” Same value, clearer message.


## 2. Personalization should feel like help


Panera’s research found that to guests, personalization means “help me.” Its system can run more than 4,000 offer combinations. But it never says, “We missed you at lunch on Tuesday.” It says, “Hey, miss you,” and offers $3 off. Helpful, not creepy.


[Jeremy Halek](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeremy-halek-7aa99458/) of the Cleveland Cavaliers showed the same care. When his team worked with


[Blings](https://www.blings.io/) to make personalized season recap videos for ticket holders, they built them around the wins each fan saw in person, not how much the fan spent. Clicks came in at 10 times the benchmark.


## 3. Faster rewards build stronger habits


[Len Covello](https://www.linkedin.com/in/len-covello/) of


[Engage People](https://engagepeople.com/) called it the 10-second rule. Points matter most at the moment someone decides where to spend. The longer a reward takes, the less it is worth to them.


[Kevin Butler](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kevin-butler-98a9338/) of United MileagePlus put it best. You would never train a dog by saying, “Good sit. I’ll get you that treat in six to eight weeks.” Yet many programs still post rewards that slowly. Speed and a steady rhythm build trust.


## 4. Your data is bigger than your program


Tractor Supply has 37 million members and $11 billion in loyalty-supported sales. But


[Shamba Schmidt](https://www.linkedin.com/in/shamba-schmidt-clmp-28888a/) of


[Epsilon](https://www.epsilon.com/us) said its real win is how it uses the data. Loyalty insights now help pick store locations, choose which products to stock and plan media spend.


Then Shamba asked the room a simple question. Whose loyalty program sits in marketing? Nearly every hand went up. Whose loyalty data shapes decisions outside marketing? Almost every hand went down. “You don’t have a CFO problem,” she said. “You have a data silo problem.”


## 5. Prove it in the language of the business


NALA’s first


[Inside Loyalty report](https://the-nala.com/inside-loyalty/) found that **85%** of senior loyalty leaders say relevance or trust is their top priority. Yet most measure revenue and visits, and only **4%** measure advocacy. We say we value trust, but we report transactions.


The fix is to tie loyalty to lifetime value and retention, the way American Express and Costco treat loyalty as part of their business model. Katie Dalton of Audience Rewards closed the day with the reminder we all needed: “Loving something and choosing it are completely different things.” Emotion matters, but it still has to show up in the numbers.


## Why attendees want to come back


Here is the fun part. The lessons from the stage showed up in our own feedback. Attendees did not rave about swag or perks. They talked about relevance, honesty and trust, the same things that make a loyalty program work. Not one person said they wouldn’t return, and **77%** of all session ratings were Excellent or Outstanding.


In our survey, attendees said:


“Finally a conference focused on loyalty. It was so great to be around like professionals and learn that we are not alone in our challenges.”


“Keep the roundtable discussions… loved it! You have created a better conference model.”


“The short presentations are perfect, enough to get the point across but not long enough to get too lost in the details.”


We also caught up with a few attendees on camera during the day.


“I’ve been to a lot of different loyalty conferences over the past few years, and this one literally has been the best one yet. Hands down, it’s the most collaborative. Great information. Don’t feel sold to.”


***Jennifer Shook** , Boehringer Ingelheim*


“This is the kind of conference that I’ve been craving in North America, especially in the States. I’ve been in loyalty for 12 plus years. So, keep doing it. I’m excited for next year.”


***Alex Stribling** , Chick-fil-A*


“We’ve been able to have really transparent, interesting conversations about our shared challenges. And it’s so interesting how consistent it can be across different types of companies.”


***Emeline Berlind** , Sephora*


“People are sharing their ideas. They’re sharing what excites them. They’re also sharing the problems that we’re seeing across the space and ways that they’re overcoming them.”


***Kate McDonough** , 7 Brew*


That is exactly why we built this: when brands share openly, everyone gets better
